confucian-junzi: In Confucian thought, the junzi is the exemplary or noble person, an ideal of moral maturity that anyone can aspire to through cultivation rather than a status fixed by noble birth. The junzi embodies virtues such as ren (humaneness), yi (rightness), and li (propriety), acting from a settled sense of what is right rather than from calculation of advantage. Confucius offered this figure as a standard for personal conduct and public leadership, contrasting the junzi with the petty person who is guided by profit and self-interest.
rectification-of-names: The rectification of names is the Confucian idea that social and moral order depends on making words match reality, so that a ruler truly rules, a father truly acts as a father, and each role is filled according to its proper meaning. Confucius argued that when names and actualities drift apart, language loses its force, obligations become unclear, and society falls into disorder. The remedy is to align conduct with the standards implied by one's titles and relationships, treating accurate naming as the foundation of good government and ethics.
mencius-good-nature: Mencius held that human nature is fundamentally good, arguing that everyone is born with incipient moral tendencies he called the four sprouts—compassion, shame, courtesy, and a sense of right and wrong. On this view wrongdoing arises not from an evil nature but from neglect, bad circumstances, or failure to nurture these innate beginnings, much as a plant withers without care. The task of ethics is therefore to cultivate and extend these natural feelings so they mature into the full virtues, a position that shaped later Confucian debates about moral education.
xunzi-bad-nature: Xunzi took the opposing Confucian view that human nature is bad, or at least unruly, since people are born with self-interested desires that, left unchecked, lead to conflict and disorder. For Xunzi goodness is not innate but a deliberate achievement, produced by ritual, education, and the accumulated wisdom of the sages, which reshape raw impulses into virtuous conduct. His emphasis on ritual (li) and conscious effort as the source of morality directly answered Mencius's claim that virtue grows from natural sprouts.
taoism: Taoism (Daoism) is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in harmony with the Tao, the underlying pattern and source of all things. Associated with the Daodejing attributed to Laozi and the writings of Zhuangzi, it prizes spontaneity, simplicity, and naturalness over rigid convention, striving, and artificial control. As a philosophy it counsels yielding to the natural course of events rather than forcing outcomes, and it later developed into organized religious forms with their own practices and pursuit of longevity.
the-tao: The Tao, or the Way, is the central notion of Daoism: the nameless, formless source and ordering principle from which all things arise and to which they return. In the Daodejing, associated with Laozi, the Tao is said to be beyond full description or definition—"the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao"—yet it can be sensed and followed by those who cultivate stillness and simplicity. Living well means aligning oneself with this natural course rather than resisting it through force, ambition, or excessive contrivance.
wu-wei: Wu wei, often translated as effortless action or non-forcing, is the Daoist ideal of acting in accordance with the natural flow of things rather than against it. It does not mean doing nothing, but acting without strain, coercion, or self-assertive striving, so that one's conduct arises spontaneously and fits the situation, as water finds its own path around obstacles. Associated with Laozi and the Daodejing, wu wei holds that the most effective and harmonious results come from restraint and responsiveness rather than aggressive control.
zhuangzi-perspectivism: Zhuangzi is known for a playful perspectivism that questions whether any single viewpoint can capture the truth about reality or value. His famous butterfly-dream story—waking unsure whether he is a man who dreamt he was a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming he is a man—dramatizes how our judgments about what is real, right, or beautiful depend on the standpoint we occupy. Rather than settling such disputes, Zhuangzi urges a flexible, open acceptance of the constant transformation of things, loosening our grip on fixed distinctions and rigid certainties.
yin-yang: Yin and yang name a pair of complementary forces that, in Chinese thought, underlie all change and balance in the natural and social world. Yin is associated with qualities such as darkness, receptivity, and rest, and yang with light, activity, and assertion, but neither is good or evil; each contains a seed of the other and continually gives way to it. This idea offers a way of understanding reality as a dynamic interplay of opposites that must be kept in harmony rather than a battle in which one side must triumph.
sun-tzu-strategy: Attributed to Sun Tzu in The Art of War, this approach holds that the highest form of strategy achieves its aims with minimal fighting, ideally subduing an opponent without direct battle at all. It stresses knowledge, preparation, deception, timing, and adapting to circumstances, so that victory is secured through positioning and foresight rather than brute force. Though framed for warfare, its counsel to win by shaping conditions in advance has been widely applied to politics, business, and everyday conflict.
buddhism: Buddhism is a family of traditions arising from the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, in ancient India, aimed at understanding and ending suffering. It diagnoses ordinary existence as marked by dissatisfaction rooted in craving and ignorance, and it offers a path of ethical conduct, mental discipline, and insight leading toward liberation, often described as nirvana. Rejecting reliance on a creator deity for salvation, Buddhism emphasizes practices such as meditation and the cultivation of wisdom and compassion, and it has developed into diverse schools across Asia and beyond.
four-noble-truths: The Four Noble Truths form the core framework of the Buddha's teaching about suffering and its resolution. They state that life is pervaded by suffering or unsatisfactoriness (dukkha), that this suffering arises from craving and attachment, that it can cease when craving is extinguished, and that there is a path—the Noble Eightfold Path—leading to that cessation. Presented like a physician's diagnosis and cure, they set out both the problem of human dissatisfaction and a practical program for overcoming it.
buddhist-impermanence: Impermanence, or anicca, is the Buddhist teaching that all conditioned things are in constant flux, arising and passing away without any stable, lasting essence. Nothing—no object, feeling, thought, or self—remains fixed, and clinging to what is inherently changing is a central source of suffering. Recognizing impermanence is meant to loosen attachment and foster acceptance, and it stands alongside suffering and non-self as one of the three marks of existence in Buddhist thought.
buddhist-non-self: Non-self, or anatman, is the Buddhist claim that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul underlying our experience. What we take to be a fixed "I" is, on this view, a shifting bundle of physical and mental processes that continually arise and dissolve, held together only by habit and craving. Understanding non-self is intended to undercut the self-centered grasping that drives suffering, and it distinguishes Buddhism from traditions that posit an enduring soul.
buddhist-karma: In Buddhist thought, karma is the principle that intentional actions carry moral consequences that shape one's future experience and, across the cycle of rebirth, one's future existences. Wholesome intentions and deeds tend toward better outcomes while harmful ones lead to suffering, so character and circumstance are understood as the ripening of past choices rather than the decree of a judging deity. Bound up with rebirth, karma explains the continuity of moral cause and effect through successive lives, until liberation frees one from the cycle altogether.
